# The Last Frame — Chapter Outline (Book 1)

*Revised October 26, 2026 after independent reviews (see Revision log at the end).*

---

## Structure overview

**Total chapters:** 10
**Target word count:** ~32,000 (Chapters 01–09 run 3,200–3,600; Chapter 10 runs ~2,000)
**POV:** Dual close-third. Odd chapters are Ellen's and even chapters are Ray's, with three exceptions:
- Chapter 08 is Ray's, with one short Ellen section.
- Chapter 09 is mostly Ellen's, with one Ray section at the end for the key.
- Chapter 10 is Ellen's for Monday, March 1, and Ray's for the short April coda (he is up the ladder at the sign).

I kept the brief's default because the story depends on the reader seeing both sides of the dark moment and agreeing with each.
**Calendar:** Tuesday, December 1 to Monday, March 1, plus a short coda at ice-out in April. The weekdays match the 2026–27 calendar: Dec 1 is a Tuesday, Feb 27 is a Saturday, March 1 is a Monday. The prose never needs to name the year.
**Act breaks:**
- Act 1 ends after Chapter 02 (~21%), when Ellen turns down Ray's buyout. That is the point of no return.
- Midpoint at Chapter 05 (~51%), with the first kiss and then the ledger discovery.
- Act 2 ends after Chapter 07 (~72%), the dark moment.
- Act 3 covers Chapters 08–10.

### The spine in one line
Ellen spent 31 years making sure nothing unexpected ever happened. Ray has spent six years making sure nothing changes. A candlepin alley teaches them both the game's one mercy: **the wood stays on the lane, and you play what's left.**

### The two wants (they can't both be fully met)
- **Ellen** wants to make Kettle Lanes pay **on her own** by March 1. Mandatory retirement at 56 was the one big change in her life she didn't choose. This is the first one she did choose, and she needs to know she can carry it. To make it pay, she has to change the alley.
- **Ray** wants to **own the alley and keep it as it was.** It was what he'd planned for the rest of his life once his son took over the hardware store. It is also the last place where things are still the way they were when his wife Linda was alive. His financing came through eight days after the alley was sold to Ellen. If she defaults, his right of first refusal gives him the alley.

Neither of them is the villain, and no single honest conversation dissolves the conflict. By Chapter 07 they have had that conversation, and they still want incompatible things.

### Ray's decency, made visible early
The reader has to trust Ray from page one even while he stands to profit from Ellen's failure. Four anchors carry that:
- He has no square in the town's pool on when Ellen folds. The pool hangs behind his own register and he won't buy one (Ch 01).
- He never enters her building uninvited. In Ch 01 he knocks with Arlene's key in his fist rather than use it. After she rekeys, every after-hours visit is either cleared by text (Ch 02) or logged on her strip under their deal (Ch 03 onward).
- When the league meeting turns on Ellen (Ch 07), he stands beside her at the counter, while still disagreeing with her and still holding his right of first refusal.
- He never puts money in, and he never lets a machine stay broken, even after the breakup (Ch 08).

## The deadline (money and the championship)

**How the purchase works** (the bible's Money table is authoritative):
- The purchase price was about $390,000. Ellen paid roughly $140,000 down from savings and the sale of her house. Arlene, the former owner, **carries a $250,000 note, interest-only at 6% ($1,250 a month), with the balloon due March 1.** She needs the cash for her entrance fee at a continuing-care retirement community, which is why the term is short.
- Ellen's plan is to refinance with Granite Lakes Savings Bank. The banker will write the loan only if two things are true:
  1. **The winter quarter (Dec 1 to Feb 28) produces at least $30,000 in net operating income.** Last winter under Arlene it produced about $21,000.
  2. **Ellen has at least $25,000 in cash on hand on Feb 28** (a working-capital requirement). She starts with $42,000.
- If she misses either one, she can't pay Arlene on March 1, so she has to sell, and **Ray's recorded right of first refusal** means any sale goes to him first. He's the only buyer with financing ready. The town's version: "If she misses, she has to sell, and Ray gets first crack."
- **The championship** is the league's final night, traditionally the last Saturday of February (Feb 27). It is the Linda Gagnon Memorial, Ray's late wife's trophy, and it is the last big revenue night before the bank looks at the numbers.

**How it tightens, chapter by chapter** (the bible's revised Money table is authoritative for every figure; the cash column below has been updated to match it)

| Ch | Net income pace vs. $30K | Cash vs. $25K floor | What moved it |
|----|----------------------------|----------------------|---------------|
| 01 | Starts at 0, 13 weeks left | $42,000 | Lane 7 dies on night one, and league fees for that lane are refunded |
| 02 | Behind | $41,000 | Lane 7 is down for two days. Restocking |
| 03 | About 90% of pace | $34,300 | Ellen starts paying Ray as a mechanic, a real cost Arlene never booked. December office parties and the new Friday glow night add revenue |
| 04 | About 95% | $36,650 | The snowed-in league night turns a profit, but the storm closes the alley for two days |
| 05 | About 99% of pace, a false victory | $38,800 (projected ~$45,000) | The sold-out holiday Saturday. **Then the ledger:** league nights lose about $700 a week because the lineage rate has been frozen since 2004 and the alley pays the prize-fund extras. Projected finish: about $26,000 |
| 06 | Projected about $24,000 | $15,150 actual; projected **$19,000** | The old cast-iron boiler cracks from age on an ordinary January night. Replacement costs $24,500 in cash, plus emergency heaters and a closed day. Ellen moves the championship into a public "Kettle Open" on derby weekend, with paid entries, spectators, and a raffle split with the derby |
| 07 | Projected about $22,000 | $15,150 actual; projected about $17,000 | She raises league lineage and two teams quit in protest, which means lost league revenue |
| 08 | Projected about $29,000 | Projected about $23,750 | Ray brings both teams back at the new rate. Open entries sell out. February vacation week is strong. A storm forecast puts derby weekend at risk |
| 09 | **Final through Feb 28: $30,850** | **Final Feb 28: $25,600** | The storm-day Open. The derby's indoor events move to the alley, as planned in Ch 06 |
| 10 | Bank approves March 1 | Note paid | Judy approves Monday morning; same-day closing; Arlene paid by wire |

The final margin is small, and every dollar of it comes from something Ellen decided earlier: pricing, the glow night, the derby partnership, and the league rate. No windfall closes the gap and nobody rescues her. Ray never puts money in.

## Romance beats

| Beat | Chapter | Where it happens |
|------|---------|------------------|
| Meet-hostile | 01 | Ray knocks with Arlene's key in his fist and won't hand it over. Ellen calls the only locksmith in town to rekey, which turns out to be Gagnon & Son. Then her ceremonial first ball hops into his lane and destroys his frame in front of 40 league bowlers |
| Hostile respect | 02 | He rekeys her lock against himself and hands over every new key. That night he fixes lane 7 after clearing it with her by text |
| Forced proximity | 03 → 04 | The key deal, paid mechanic calls, and 7 a.m. bowling lessons (Ch 03), then the snowed-in league night (Ch 04) |
| First real laugh together | 04 | 2 a.m., power out, both of them crouched in the pit behind lane 5 setting pins by hand |
| **Kiss 1** | 05 | After close on the sold-out Saturday, under the neon sign with the dead "K" |
| **Kiss 2** | 06 | 3 a.m. in the basement, just the two of them, waiting for the certified oil-heat technician while Ellen holds the flashlight on the cracked boiler |
| First real break | 06 | The argument over what she promised in Ch 03 |
| Dark moment | 07 | Ray offers to buy in as a partner. Ellen refuses because she has to know she can carry it. Ray, equally honest, keeps his right of first refusal. At the meeting he stands beside her anyway. Afterward she owns her part in one plain line, and they are still apart |
| Strained | 08 | A machine fails during vacation week. He comes in, fixes it, hands her an invoice. Neither mentions the breakup |
| Grand gesture, private | 08 | Ray releases his right of first refusal at Arlene's lawyer's office, then bowls a side match at the rival alley to win back the two teams that quit |
| Ellen's answering gesture | 09 | Before the final, before the bank decides, and before she knows about the release, she gives Ray a relief briefing and asks him to share the position (the D-side). She can still lose everything when she asks |
| Grand gesture, public | 09 | Ray gives Linda's trophy to the Open by PA request. After the Open he returns the key she chose to give him, with the signed release. She puts it back in his hand |
| **Kiss 3 (declaration)** | 10 | Monday afternoon, after the closing, in the pit behind lane 7. Ray says "I love you," important words last. She says it back, plainly |
| Coda | 10 | April. Ray fixes the dead K and Ellen lets him. Denise refuses to sell Ellen the "wedding date" square. **Kiss 4 is optional** here; the drafter may leave it out |

**Kiss count: three firm (Ch 05, Ch 06, Ch 10), one optional (Ch 10 coda). Four at most, per the bible.**

## Supporting cast (three with real weight)

- **Denise Lavoie, 61.** She has run the Kettle Lanes counter for 22 years and is the best woman bowler in town. She's divorced and dry-witted. She starts as Ellen's skeptic and becomes her friend. **Book 2 lead.** Her Book 1 thread closes when her team wins the Linda Gagnon trophy in Ch 09. Seed only: one exchange in Ch 08 with Gil Arsenault, 63, the widowed owner of the rival alley, and one line from Gil at the Open in Ch 09 when she wins.
- **Hollis Pike, 66.** A retired NH Fish and Game conservation officer who runs a plow route in winter and chairs the ice-fishing derby. He is Ray's best friend and teammate. **Book 3 lead.** His Book 1 thread, getting the derby through the storm, closes in Ch 09. Seed only: Hollis and Judy Ostrowski at the derby weigh-in on lane 10 in Ch 09 (Judy ice-fishes).
- **Arlene Fortier, 84.** Owned the alley from 1971 to 2026. She holds the note and gave Ray the right of first refusal out of guilt. She explains in Ch 08 why she chose Ellen. Her thread closes when she is paid on March 1 (Ch 10) and moves into the retirement community.

**Minor characters (no weight, one or two scenes each):** Kate Daly, 31, Ellen's daughter, an ER nurse in Manchester (Ellen's side of a phone call in Ch 02, in person in Ch 09). Danny Gagnon, 35, Ray's son, who runs the hardware store day to day (Ch 01 by phone, Ch 02, and Ch 08, where he gets the store outright). Judy Ostrowski, the banker at Granite Lakes Savings (Ch 03, Ch 09 weigh-in, Ch 10). Gil Arsenault (Ch 08, one line in Ch 09). Verna Tibbetts, 88, league secretary (Ch 07, and the substitute ruling in Ch 09).

**Walk-ons stay unnamed:** Arlene's lawyer, the defectors' anchor, the three regulars on the Bench at the hardware store, the technician, the party guests.

**Threads Book 1 raises, and where each one closes:** the note (10) · the right of first refusal (signed away 08, revealed 09) · the league rate and the two teams that quit (08, with a sour line in 09) · the championship and Linda's trophy (09) · Ray's keys (01 knock, 02 rekey, 03 deal, 09 return) · locker 14 (08) · the pool on when Ellen folds (10) and its "wedding date" square (10 coda) · Danny and the store (08) · Kate's doubts (09) · Arlene's move (10) · the derby (09) · seeds: Denise–Gil (08, 09) and Hollis–Judy (09).

## Chapter 01 — Cleared to Bowl

| Field | Content |
|-------|---------|
| **POV / dates** | Ellen. Tuesday, December 1 |
| **Target words** | 3,400 |
| **Purpose** | Establish Ellen, the alley, the town, and the stakes. Inciting incident (she owns it now) and meet-hostile |
| **Opens with** | 3:40 p.m. Ellen has owned Kettle Lanes for six hours. She is labeling the lane-light switches with masking tape and a Sharpie in flight-strip format. Ten lanes, a 1958 building, and the smell of lane wood and pinsetter grease. League starts at 6:30. |
| **Key event** | At 5:15 Ray Gagnon knocks on the front door with Arlene's key in his fist. He has opened this door on every league night since 1996, and today he knocks. He declines to hand the key over. Ellen calls the only locksmith listed in town to rekey. Danny answers at Gagnon & Son and says the locksmith is his father, who is standing in her alley; he books "the locksmith" for 8 a.m. tomorrow. That night the lane 7 pinsetter dies mid-match. Ray says Arlene's mechanic was him and that this is "not my alley." Ellen runs the league on nine lanes and refunds lane 7. At close, Denise shows her the pool sheet from the hardware store with dates for when Ellen will fold. March 1 is the one square nobody has bought. Ray won't buy one; the sheet hangs behind his own register. |
| **What changes** | Ellen knows the terms the town already knows: the balloon payment, Ray's right of first refusal, and that the only man who can keep her machines running wants the building. She has lost money on night one. |
| **Emotional beat** | Delight in her competence and her deadpan, with a sting of humiliation underneath, and a first unwilling note of respect for a man who knocks. |
| **Chapter promise** | Can she run this place without the one man who knows how, and what kind of man wants her building but won't bet against her? |
| **Set piece (Ellen ATC set piece 1 of 3)** | Ellen gives lane assignments over the PA in approach-control phraseology ("Lane four, cleared to bowl"), and the league heckles her in fake pilot-speak. Hollis asks her to throw a ceremonial first ball. She lofts it past the lob line, it hops the gutter cap into lane 6, and it wipes out the wood Ray had carefully left for his third ball. Verna and the captains rule on the spot: re-rack, re-bowl the frame. |
| **Romance beat** | Meet-hostile (the knock and the key, the locksmith call, then the ruined frame) |
| **Get right** | Candlepin ball and pin sizes. The lob line and lofting fouls. Three balls per frame with deadwood staying on the lane. Lane-light and foul-light controls. Bowl-Mor-style pinsetter failure points. Approach-control phraseology ("cleared," "say again," "unable"). Basic league-night structure: teams of 4–5, three strings per bowler. Small-town hardware stores doubling as the only locksmith. |
| **Note** | Introduce the financing terms through the pool sheet and Denise's commentary, not as a summary. Ellen's backstory (FAA, mandatory retirement at 56) should arrive in single lines, not paragraphs. Denise's line about Ray and the March 1 square stays short and unexplained; let the reader do the arithmetic. |

## Chapter 02 — Right of First Refusal

| Field | Content |
|-------|---------|
| **POV / dates** | Ray. Wednesday–Thursday, December 2–3 |
| **Target words** | 3,200 |
| **Purpose** | The rival's side. Ray's want, made sympathetic. The end of Act 1 and the point of no return |
| **Opens with** | 6 a.m. at Gagnon & Son Hardware. Ray is cutting a key for a plow driver. The bank's commitment letter on an SBA loan is folded in his shirt pocket, dated eight days after Arlene accepted Ellen's offer. On Danny's tablet, the 8 a.m. job reads "Kettle Lanes, rekey, all exterior." |
| **Key event** | At 7:30 Ellen comes in with a parts list printed from a candlepin forum and a phone recording of lane 7 failing. At 8 Ray rekeys her lock against himself, properly, and hands her every new key. Arlene's 1996 key, orange tag and all, now opens nothing, and it stays on his ring. Kneeling at her lock, he offers to buy her out at exactly what she paid, so she loses nothing and walks away clean. Kate calls in the middle of it; Ray hears Ellen's half ("Kate. I'm aware."). It is a fair, sensible offer, and Kate tells her to take it. Ellen refuses. She tells him the truth: retiring at 56 was federal law, not her choice, and this is the first thing she has chosen in two years. Ray: "Then I'll see you March first." That evening he texts her that the Thursday league needs lane 7 and he can do it tonight. She replies with a time and unlocks the back door for him at nine, then goes home. In the morning the broken part is on her desk with a tag written in her own strip format. |
| **What changes** | The lines are drawn: both of them want the same building, and both say so out loud. Ellen is committed past the point of a clean exit. Ray has helped her, with her permission, and he can't explain to himself why. |
| **Emotional beat** | Sympathy for the man who lost by eight days, and pleasure at the tag on the desk. |
| **Chapter promise** | Why is Ray helping the woman whose failure gets him what he wants? |
| **Set piece (Ray's comic engines: diagnosis by sound, the Bench)** | Ellen plays the lane 7 recording on her phone at the hardware counter. Ray listens once, with his eyes closed, and names the part from the sound ("That's not the table. That's the clutch letting go a half-second late."). The three regulars on the Bench call the exchange like a broadcast and offer rival diagnoses as color commentary. Ellen reads his instructions back once; Ray waits for a readback that never comes the second time, because she has already written it down. |
| **Romance beat** | Hostility with respect showing underneath. The first time each of them is honest with the other. |
| **Get right** | Hardware-store realities in a lake town in winter: rock salt, roof rakes, plow parts, key cutting. Rekeying a commercial door (repinning the cylinder rather than replacing the lock). SBA 7(a) lender commitment timing. How a right of first refusal works when it's tied to a seller-carried note. Which pinsetter parts are scarce, and that they get scavenged from closed alleys. |
| **Pacing flag** | Act 1 ends at about 21%, slightly early. That works because the purchase happens before page one, but Ch 01 has to carry a lot of setup without dumping it. If Ch 01 runs long, move the pool-sheet reveal to Ray's register in Ch 02: he sees the empty March 1 square every morning and doesn't buy it. Ch 02 is also busy (store, rekey, offer, Kate, night repair). The rekey and the offer share one scene to save room. |

## Chapter 03 — Deadwood

| Field | Content |
|-------|---------|
| **POV / dates** | Ellen. December 8–19 |
| **Target words** | 3,300 |
| **Purpose** | First complications and forced proximity. Ellen starts operating, and the deadline becomes a hard number |
| **Opens with** | Judy Ostrowski at Granite Lakes Savings slides a single sheet across her desk with two numbers circled: $30,000 and $25,000. |
| **Key event** | Ellen and Ray make a deal. He keeps the machines running and she pays him a fair per-call rate on proper invoices. She insists, pointing out that his free labor is one reason Arlene's numbers looked better than they were. **The key becomes part of the deal:** she gives him one of the new keys for after-hours repair calls, and pins a strip to her board headed R.G. — AFTER HOURS, with columns for date, time in, time out, lane, and reason. He logs every visit in his square capitals. He also teaches her to bowl, because Denise has told her an owner who can't bowl gets no respect from the league. **Ray's price is a promise:** the championship stays as it has always been, the last Saturday of February, all ten lanes. Ellen gives her word that it stays as it is "unless the numbers say otherwise." Ray hears the first half. |
| **What changes** | They are now in business together, and she holds a key arrangement she designed. She has made a promise whose second half Ray didn't register. She has priced the alley properly, starting a Friday glow night and sequencing December office parties. |
| **Emotional beat** | Comic friction warming into something neither of them will name. A faint chill at the promise, because the reader heard both halves. |
| **Chapter promise** | Will the numbers say otherwise, and what happens when Ray finds out what she actually promised? |
| **Set piece** | 7 a.m. lessons. Ellen brings a clipboard and calculates entry angles. Ray tells her to stop doing math at the pins. Her lofted balls skip like stones. Ray teaches her what to do with deadwood: "The wood stays on the lane. You play what's left." (Full line, use 1 of 3.) She keeps a strip board at the counter, and every party booking gets a flight strip. |
| **Romance beat** | Forced proximity, part 1. Their first touch is him correcting her release. |
| **Plants (required)** | Judy orders the appraisal and environmental review now, so a March 1 same-day closing is possible. Denise makes Ellen buy a league sanction card "so you're legal if they're ever short" (pays off in Ch 09). Ellen opens a separate account for meals tax, prize-fund money, and anything she is only holding (pays off in Ch 10). The promise must be on the page word for word, including "unless the numbers say otherwise," with Ray mid-motion (setting a pin, checking a belt) so a reader can believe he missed the tail. |
| **Get right** | Candlepin technique: hitting the 1–3 pocket versus the headpin, "chop," using deadwood. Named leaves (four-horse, spread eagle, half worcester; use names without pin numbers). Strike, spare, and ten-box scoring. The perfect game is 300 and has never been bowled; the best anyone has done is 245. Small-business bank refinance criteria: debt service coverage and liquidity. Paper flight strips and strip bays (Ellen's tower years). |

## Chapter 04 — Ground Stop

| Field | Content |
|-------|---------|
| **POV / dates** | Ray. Thursday, January 7 (Christmas has passed off the page; Author decision 8) |
| **Target words** | 3,200 |
| **Purpose** | The forced-proximity peak. Ray falls, and knows it. |
| **Opens with** | Hollis's plow stuck sideways at the bottom of Kettle Lanes' driveway with the blade down, at 8:50 p.m., while snow comes down faster than he can push it. |
| **Key event** | A nor'easter closes the roads during the Thursday league, and 31 bowlers are stranded overnight. Ellen declares a ground stop, assigns sleeping spots in sequence, runs the snack bar on rations, and turns the night into a paid all-night marathon: the house keeps the lineage and the snack bar and adds a set amount to the prize fund. Then the power goes out. With no pinsetters, Ray and Ellen get into the pit behind lane 5 and set pins by hand while Denise bowls by flashlight. He tells her about Linda's 1998 record on the wall. She tells him about her last day on the scope. |
| **What changes** | They are friends. Ray knows now that he's been rooting for her for weeks. The night made money even with the storm. |
| **Emotional beat** | Warmth, laughter, and the first ache of tenderness. |
| **Chapter promise** | What happens to these two when the snow stops? |
| **Set piece (Ray's comic engine: "Fella I knew…")** | "Candlepin by candlelight." Two people around 60 in the pit, dodging flying wood, while 31 bowlers in parkas heckle them. Between strings, Ray's "Fella I knew…" stories become the night's entertainment: the stranded bowlers start requesting them by topic, and Ellen asks for the source on every one ("Which fella?"). Their first real laugh together comes when a deadwood pin rolls into Ray's lap and Ellen calls "traffic, twelve o'clock, one mile." |
| **Romance beat** | Forced proximity, part 2. First real laugh together. |
| **Get right** | Hand-setting candlepins (pinspotter history, pin deck positions). What happens to a pinsetter in a power cut. Nor'easter behavior in the Lakes Region. Municipal versus contract plowing. Ground-stop language (Ch 04 is not an Ellen set piece: three ATC phrases at most). The FAA 2-2-1 "rattler" shift schedule (her last day). Power cut stops the oil boiler, so everyone sleeps in parkas. NH emergency-shelter norms (don't overdo them). The 31 bowlers make the overnight plainly chaperoned. |

## Chapter 05 — The Push (Midpoint)

| Field | Content |
|-------|---------|
| **POV / dates** | Ellen. Saturday, January 16 (holiday weekend) |
| **Target words** | 3,200 |
| **Purpose** | Midpoint: a false victory, then a reversal. Before it, Ellen is winning over the town with Ray's help. After it, the road to winning runs straight through Ray's league. |
| **Opens with** | 9:58 a.m. A line of eleven-year-olds in rental shoes runs out the door, and Ellen has a handheld radio clipped to her collar. |
| **Key event** | The first sold-out Saturday. Ellen sequences it like the evening arrival push into Logan, and they kiss under the neon sign after close. Then she reconciles December and January against Arlene's old ledgers. League lineage has been frozen since 2004, the alley quietly pays for the league banquet and prize extras, and league nights lose about $700 a week. Even at today's pace she finishes around $26,000. The thing sinking the alley is Ray's league. She said "unless the numbers say otherwise," and the numbers now say it. She also knows which half of that sentence Ray heard. |
| **What changes** | The story turns. Ellen now has to choose between the alley and the promise the man she just kissed believes she made. |
| **Emotional beat** | Elation, then a cold drop. |
| **Chapter promise** | Will she tell him, and what will he do when she does? |
| **Set piece (Ellen ATC set piece 2 of 3)** | Three birthday parties, a youth hockey team, the Rotary, and the retirement party for the Ambrose Elementary lunch staff, all at once. Ray is on the machines and they talk over handheld radios ("Kettle Maintenance, say intentions." / "Intentions are to quit."). The party pizzas arrive as a logistics problem; Denise grades the rental shoes of eleven-year-olds out loud. |
| **Romance beat** | Kiss 1 |
| **Get right** | League economics: what lineage is, how prize funds and sanction fees work, and the $7.50 rate frozen since 2004 (invented figure; keep it to the ledger scene). Birthday-party pricing at small alleys. Arrival-push sequencing and miles-in-trail. |
| **Note** | No withheld secret. Ellen decides by the last line of the chapter to tell him tomorrow, and she does it in Ch 06. |

## Chapter 06 — Holding Pattern

| Field | Content |
|-------|---------|
| **POV / dates** | Ray. Sunday, January 17 – Monday, February 1 |
| **Target words** | 3,500 |
| **Purpose** | Escalating complications. The conflict comes into the open, a cost shock forces Ellen to act, and the couple gets its one private night before the break. |
| **Opens with** | Dawn on Sunday, January 17, the morning after the kiss, in Hollis's bob-house on Great Kettle Lake. The auger hole is skimming over, a tip-up flag is down, and Hollis asks whether Ray is "courting." |
| **Key event** | Ellen tells Ray about the ledger plainly that afternoon: "Your league costs me seven hundred dollars a week." He takes it hard and offers to raise rates next season, but she needs it now. Late in January, on an ordinary weeknight, Ray is in after league on a logged call for lane 3's clutch when he hears the boiler fail from the pit: a cast-iron section, cracked from age. He calls Ellen. She works a checklist, not a toolbox: a certified oil-heat technician, two hours out; water shut off to the boiler; rented heaters booked for morning. **At 3 a.m. it is only the two of them in the basement, waiting**, Ellen holding the flashlight on a machine neither of them is allowed to touch. Kiss 2 happens there. The bill is $24,500 out of her cash, plus heaters and one closed day. With her cash projection now below the floor, she draws up the Kettle Open: on Feb 27 the championship becomes the final round of a public open on derby weekend, with entries, spectators, and a shared raffle. If the ice is unsafe, the derby's indoor events move to the alley. She tells Ray before anyone else and asks him to help her sell it to the league. **The argument is over what she promised.** He says she gave her word. She says she gave it "unless the numbers say otherwise," and the numbers did. He says he never heard that part. She says she said it. Both of them are telling the truth. He says no. Then she walks out onto the ice to pitch the derby committee, and Ray, already in Hollis's bob-house, watches her win the room he just refused her. |
| **What changes** | Ellen has changed the championship, openly and for a reason, on the terms she actually stated. Ray has to decide whether a promise he only half heard still binds her, and what the alley is to him. |
| **Emotional beat** | Tenderness in the basement, then the floor dropping out from under them. |
| **Chapter promise** | Can they still be together if they want opposite things for the same place? |
| **Set piece (Hollis's comic engine)** | The derby pitch belongs to Hollis. Before he lets Ellen off the public access, he measures the ice with a spud bar and a tape and reads her the numbers. At the bob-house door he questions her like a license check: name, address, purpose of visit, number of lines in the water, whether she has a plan if the ice goes. She hands him a printed plan with contingencies, which no one in derby history has done. Mid-pitch two tip-up flags pop. Ellen's one line: "Stand by." She lands the fish. Hollis writes something in his waterproof notebook and asks what Plan B is. |
| **Romance beat** | Kiss 2. Courtship in the open (the pool sheet gets a new square: "wedding date"), then the first real break |
| **Get right** | NH ice-fishing rules: lines per angler, bob-house removal deadlines, species. How an ice-fishing derby runs, with weigh-ins and safety calls (do not copy the real Meredith derby). How an old cast-iron oil boiler fails from age (a cracked section, water on the floor), replacement cost and timing. NH oil-heat technician certification (voluntary; Ellen hires "a certified oil-heat technician"; never call it a required license). Freeze protection for a commercial building. NH conservation-officer license-check routine. |
| **Pacing flag** | Still the most crowded chapter: bob-house dawn, the ledger talk, the boiler night, the argument, and the derby pitch. The parka league night has been cut from it. If it runs long, fold the ledger talk into the opening by having Ellen walk out to the bob-house that morning to tell Ray (then the pitch is her second trip onto the ice, which Hollis notes). Protect the 3 a.m. basement scene above all; it is the couple's only private time before the break. |

## Chapter 07 — Loss of Separation (Dark Moment)

| Field | Content |
|-------|---------|
| **POV / dates** | Ellen. Tuesday, February 2 |
| **Target words** | 3,200 |
| **Purpose** | The dark moment, coming from the leads' conflicting wants. The end of Act 2. |
| **Opens with** | 5:45 p.m. Ray is sitting in his truck in the Kettle Lanes lot with the engine running and a cashier's check for $55,000 on the dashboard. |
| **Key event** | Ray offers to buy in as an equity partner. He has the numbers (worked out with Danny on the store's adding machine): $48,000 pays the note down, which cuts her debt payments and drops Judy's income bar to about $23,950, under her $24,000 projection without touching league rates; the other $7,000 lifts her Feb 28 cash to about $26,000, over the floor. It closes both gaps and saves the championship as it was. He admits it's both: he wants her, and he still wants the alley, and he can't separate the two. Ellen refuses. If she takes it, she'll never know whether she could carry it, and he'll never know whether she wanted him or needed his money. Ray is just as honest: then he is keeping his right of first refusal, because if she fails, someone has to keep the alley open. "Then we want the same building," she says, and she ends it. **The cost comes before the podium:** twenty minutes alone in the office, and the 2 a.m. memory, the worst night of her career, handled in "the voice" while everything inside her broke. She is doing it again, and she knows it. Then the league meeting. She announces the new $12.50 lineage and the Open. The room turns on her. When two teams get up to walk out to the rival alley forty minutes away, Ray gets up too, crosses the room, and stands beside her at the counter. He says he doesn't agree with her. He stays standing there. The teams leave anyway. At close, with the lanes dark, Ellen says one plain line owning her part: she ended it in a parking lot like a briefing, and that was hers, not his. He nods, and goes home. |
| **What changes** | Ellen has lost Ray and two teams, and her projection is worse than before. Nothing about either of their wants has changed, and both of them have behaved well. She is alone in the airspace she chose. |
| **Emotional beat** | Grief, made worse because both of them are right and neither was cruel. |
| **Chapter promise** | Can she save the alley alone, and does she still want to? |
| **Set piece (lean on Verna)** | Before the turn, the league meeting runs on Robert's Rules, chaired by Verna Tibbetts, 88, in her lavender parka with the Grange gavel. She reads the minutes from 1987 in full, recognizes a motion to rename the snack bar ("seconded in 1987; it failed then, too"), and gives Ellen exactly three minutes under Article Four, timed on her own watch. Comedy first, then the turn. Later, someone adds a square to the pool sheet: "Feb 2 — they split." Denise crosses it out in pen without comment. |
| **Romance beat** | Dark moment |
| **Get right** | Equity partnership versus loan (so the scene's business logic holds; see the bible's Money table on the $55,000). League-meeting procedure and how a league changes its rates mid-season. Ellen's one operational error in 31 years: what a loss of separation is and how it was handled ("She filed the report herself. Two days off the boards. A week of retraining."). Keep it short and specific. |
| **Note** | The parka league night from the boiler outage is off the page. At most, one detail in the office scene: Denise's earflap hat on the counter hook with "112" on masking tape. Ray standing beside her is not a reconciliation; the scene should make plain that he still holds the right of first refusal and still thinks she is wrong. Her ownership line must stay one sentence and must not explain her feelings in therapeutic terms. |

## Chapter 08 — Position Relief

| Field | Content |
|-------|---------|
| **POV / dates** | Ray, with one short Ellen section. February 8–20 |
| **Target words** | 3,400 |
| **Purpose** | Act 3 begins. Ray's turn, the private half of his grand gesture, and Ellen rebuilding on her own. |
| **Opens with** | Arlene's apartment above the pharmacy, Monday, February 8. Half-packed boxes are labeled for The Pines, and Arlene has her 1996 ledger open to the line where she wrote "key to R.G." |
| **Key event** | Arlene tells Ray why she sold to Ellen even knowing his offer was coming: "You'd have kept it a museum. I wanted it to live." **Saturday, February 13, vacation week:** Ellen texts a work order for lane 4's table, "rate per our agreement." Ray comes in because he never leaves a machine broken. He logs in on her strip, fixes it, and hands her an invoice. They speak only about the machine; neither mentions the breakup. On his way out he stops at the trophy case and Linda's 1998 record and knows Linda would have entered the Open on day one. He opens locker 14, takes Linda's ball, and leaves the locker door standing open. No one comments, then or later. Tuesday he signs a release of his right of first refusal at Arlene's lawyer's office. That night he drives to the rival alley and bowls a side match to win the two teams back: if he wins, they return to Kettle Lanes at the new rate. Wednesday he tells Danny the hardware store is his. In the Ellen section, she, Denise, and Hollis build the derby-weekend contingency plan while the forecast turns ugly. |
| **What changes** | Ray has given up his path to owning the alley and his hold on keeping it the same. The league is whole again, still grumbling, and Open entries sell out. Ellen doesn't know what Ray did yet, and the story doesn't hide it from the reader. |
| **Emotional beat** | Hope that has been earned, and a lump in the throat. |
| **Chapter promise** | Will Ray tell her, and will the weather let any of this happen? |
| **Set pieces** | (1) Ray at Pine Ridge Lanes in Halsey Falls. He bowls a side match against the defectors' anchor with a borrowed house ball, refereed scrupulously by Gil. He hasn't bowled under pressure since Linda died. He starts terribly ("Holy mackerel," once, and he hears himself) and wins the tenth on deadwood: "The wood stays on the lane. You play what's left." (Full line, use 2 of 3.) Denise came as scorekeeper; this is the one-exchange seed between Denise and Gil, about a spare she picked up in 2015. (2) **Ray's comic engine, the Bench:** when Ray tells Danny the store is his, the three regulars call the handover like a broadcast, argue over who they report to now, and ask Danny whether the coffee is included. (3) In the Ellen section: a Plan A–D whiteboard. Hollis asks, "What's Plan E?" Ellen: "Plan E is we all go home." |
| **Romance beat** | Strained (the invoice). The grand gesture, private half. |
| **Get right** | Releasing a right of first refusal (Ray signs, the lawyer notarizes, "she'll record it this afternoon"). Candlepin match etiquette between rival houses. Massachusetts February vacation week brings visitors. Locker 14 stays unremarked: no speech, no flashback. |
| **Pacing flag** | Four locations and a POV switch in 3,400 words. The strained repair scene and the trophy-case beat share one visit to the alley, which saves a scene. Keep Arlene and the lawyer's office short (three details each). |

## Chapter 09 — The Last Frame

| Field | Content |
|-------|---------|
| **POV / dates** | Mostly Ellen, with one Ray section at the end. Saturday, February 27 |
| **Target words** | 3,600 |
| **Purpose** | Climax. The Open, the storm, Ellen's answering gesture while she can still lose, and the public half of Ray's. Ends on the key. |
| **Opens with** | 4:10 a.m. Saturday. Ellen is at the counter with the radar loop on her phone. Snow is blowing sideways under the parking-lot lights, and Hollis's voice on the radio is calling the derby's outdoor day. |
| **Key event** | The storm cancels fishing, and the indoor events move to the alley exactly as planned in Ch 06. Ellen runs the day like a storm day at the TRACON: holding lists, sequencing, and a ground stop on the snack bar. The returning teams pay $12.50 and grumble; one sour line from one of them, which Denise answers. By midday the day is more than one person can hold: two tables are acting up, 150 people are in snow boots, and Hollis has been called out to plow. Ellen finds Ray in the pit and, instead of briefing him, asks. She gives him a relief briefing and asks him to share the position: "At the Center they call it the D-side. We borrowed their words when ours weren't good enough." She means today and after, whatever Judy says on Monday. She does not know about the release; as far as she knows, he still gets the building if she fails. He reads her briefing back. That is his yes. Over the PA, Ray asks to give Linda's trophy to the Open ("Kettle Lanes, Gagnon. Request." / "Gagnon, say request."). With Hollis out plowing, Ray's team is a bowler short; Verna checks the bylaws and rules that Ellen, with her sanction card, may substitute. She bowls the tenth frame and uses everything left on the lane: first ball chops, second leaves wood, third uses the deadwood ("The wood stays on the lane. You play what's left." Full line, use 3 of 3). Ray's team still loses to Denise's, and Denise finally takes the trophy, to the book's one ovation. Gil, there with the derby crowd, gets one line watching her win. Kate, in person, watches her mother run the day and comes around. **Ray section, after close:** he gives Ellen back the key she gave him in Ch 03, and the signed release, dated eleven days ago. "I don't want to own it anymore. I want to be asked." She asked him before she knew. He signed before she asked. She puts the key back in his hand and closes his fingers over it. |
| **What changes** | The alley's winter is done and the numbers are whatever they are. Each of them chose the other without knowing what the other had already given up. Denise has her trophy. Kate is on her mother's side. |
| **Emotional beat** | Joyful, funny, and earned. Tears at the key. |
| **Chapter promise** | Did she make it, and will one of them finally say it? |
| **Set piece (Ellen ATC set piece 3 of 3)** | The derby weigh-in at a bowling alley: lake trout in coolers on lane 10, a raffle drawn from a ball return, and 150 people in snow boots. **Seed for Book 3:** at the lane 10 scale, Hollis weighs a lake trout Judy Ostrowski caught Friday; they talk only in measurements, and he writes her fish in his notebook twice. |
| **Romance beat** | Ellen's answering gesture (the D-side ask). The grand gesture, public half (the trophy, the key, the release). |
| **Get right** | How a derby's weather call is made and announced. Position relief briefing (Ellen's D-side ask and Ray's readback). Candlepin championship format (total pins over three strings with handicap, head-to-head on a lane pair). Substitute rules for a short-handed team (Verna and the bylaws). ATC cap here is six. |
| **Pacing flag** | Still the fullest chapter, though the bank and the coda have moved out. If it runs past 4,000, trim the derby texture before touching the D-side ask, the tenth frame, or the key. The D-side ask must stay before the final. |

## Chapter 10 — Ice-Out

| Field | Content |
|-------|---------|
| **POV / dates** | Ellen for Monday, March 1. Ray for the April coda |
| **Target words** | 2,000 (about 1,500 Monday, 500 coda) |
| **Purpose** | Resolution and the unmistakable happy ending. The bank, the note, the declaration, and a short look at them as a couple. |
| **Opens with** | 8:30 a.m. Monday. Judy's office: the bowl of butterscotch, the framed lake trout, and Ellen's books, closed Sunday night from the register reports and bank statements, squared on the desk. |
| **Key event** | Judy approves the refinance at $30,850 net operating income and $25,600 cash, and notices with approval that the meals tax, the prize-fund money, and the derby's half of the raffle sit in a separate account: "Congratulations. Don't celebrate until it funds." The closing happens that afternoon at Arlene's lawyer's office. Arlene is paid by wire, licks her thumb and counts the confirmation, and tells Ellen in one line why she chose her. Denise closes the pool on when Ellen would fold: nobody held March 1, and the pot goes to the derby's kids' division. Ellen goes back to the alley. On the strip board, Ray has logged himself in: date, time, lane 7, reason: WAITING. He is in the pit behind lane 7, where the first machine died on her first night. He calls her "Mrs. Daly," and she doesn't correct him. He tells her he loves her, important words last. She says it back, plainly and exactly, and they kiss (Kiss 3). |
| **What changes** | The alley is hers by her own numbers. Arlene is paid and gone to The Pines. Ellen and Ray are a couple by choice, with nothing left owed in either direction. |
| **Emotional beat** | Relief, then quiet happiness, then a laugh. |
| **Chapter promise** | Resolved. |
| **Coda (Ray, April ice-out)** | Great Kettle Lake goes dark at the edges and the ice turns the color of old pewter. The town's ice-out pool has replaced the fold pool; Ellen bought a square and loses. Ray is up a ladder at the road sign fixing the dead K, and Ellen, who hires out everything she isn't qualified for, lets him. At the counter she tries to buy the "wedding date" square from the old sheet; Denise refuses to sell it to her ("Honey, you don't get to bet on your own flight."). The sign comes on: KETTLE LANES, all of it. Optional Kiss 4 at the foot of the ladder; leave it out if the scene lands without it. |
| **Get right** | Refinance closing timeline and same-day funding (pre-staged in Ch 03). How a seller note is paid off by wire. Neon sign repair for a single dead letter (transformer, electrode, or a new tube from a sign shop that Ray installs; pick the plausible one). Ice-out traditions in the Lakes Region (invent our own method). |
| **Pacing flag** | The shortest chapter by design. Don't let Monday's paperwork eat the declaration; the bank scene and the closing can share a page. The last line should be an action or a line of dialogue, not a reflection. |

## Research checklist for bible-builder (consolidated)

**Candlepin**
- Ball (max ~4.5 in, about 2 lb 7 oz, no holes) and pin (~15¾ in, about 2 lb 8 oz) specs. Lane length, foul line, lob line.
- Three balls per frame. Deadwood stays on the lane. Rules for wood in the gutter. Strike, spare, ten-box scoring.
- **Maximum score is 300 and has never been bowled. The sanctioned record is 245.** The brief's "perfect 450" looks like an error. Verify before anything is drafted.
- Named leaves. Chop. Pocket strategy.
- Pinsetter make and history (Bowl-Mor), parts scarcity, and how mechanics keep them running.
- ICBA sanctioning, lineage, prize funds, and typical current league fees.
- The candlepin TV broadcasts (useful for Ray's and Arlene's memories).
- How many candlepin alleys remain and the pace of closures.
- Whether candlepin lanes are oiled or conditioned.

**Air-traffic control**
- FAA mandatory retirement at 56 (and the waiver), and the hiring age cap.
- Boston Consolidated TRACON (Merrimack, NH) versus Boston Center (Nashua). Ellen did tower years (paper strips) and then the TRACON.
- FAA phraseology (the 7110.65 conventions, e.g., "affirmative" in the US).
- Position relief briefings. Ground stops, flow control, miles-in-trail.
- The 2-2-1 schedule. Operational-error handling. Controller slang (verify before using any).
- FERS pension and the special supplement, for her financial picture.

**Winter town and business**
- NH ice-fishing law, bob-house deadlines, and derby operations. Conservation-officer license-check routine.
- Nor'easters and snow-load realities. Old cast-iron oil boiler failure from age, and replacement.
- Rekeying a commercial lock.
- NH meals tax on the snack bar. February vacation week.
- Seller-carried notes with balloon payments, rights of first refusal and their release, and small-bank refinance criteria (DSCR, liquidity).
- Continuing-care community entrance fees (Arlene's motive).
- Repairing a single dead letter on a neon sign.

## Author decisions (approved October 26, 2026)

The outline is approved as written, with these answers to the open questions:

1. **Names:** Ellen Daly (58), Ray Gagnon (61), Denise Lavoie, Hollis Pike, Arlene Fortier, Danny Gagnon, Kate Daly, Judy Ostrowski, Gil Arsenault. Keep all of them.
2. **Town:** Ambrose, New Hampshire, on Great Kettle Lake. Kettle Lanes (1958, ten lanes). The rival is Pine Ridge Lanes. Keep all of them.
3. **Backstories:** Ellen divorced amicably about 20 years ago, and her ex is never on the page. Ray's wife Linda died six years ago. Keep both.
4. **Candlepin score:** the maximum is 300, which has never been bowled. The record is reported as 245; verify it in the bible.
5. **Ending:** Ellen keeps ownership and asks Ray to share running the alley (the D-side). There is no ownership stake for Ray in book 1.
6. **Final:** Ellen's team loses and Denise's team wins the trophy.
7. **April coda:** keep it, and keep it short.
8. **Christmas:** stays off the page.
9. **Chapters:** 10 chapters (author approved Oct 26 after review).
10. **Title:** *The Last Frame*. Check Amazon for clashing titles before publishing.

## Revision log (Oct 26)

Nine author-approved changes from independent reviews:

1. **Ray made trustworthy.** No square in the fold pool (March 1 left unclaimed; he won't buy one). He stands beside Ellen at the Ch 07 meeting while still disagreeing and still holding his right of first refusal. Keys: Ch 01 knock and locksmith call (Gagnon & Son); Ch 02 rekey and a night repair cleared by text; Ch 03 key deal with a logged strip; he never enters uninvited; the Ch 09 return is of a key she chose to give him.
2. **More couple time.** Ch 06 3 a.m. basement scene and Kiss 2. Ch 08 strained repair-and-invoice scene. Parka league night cut from Ch 06.
3. **Ellen's answering gesture moved earlier.** The D-side ask comes on storm day, before the final and before the bank, without knowledge of the release. She owns her part in the breakup in one plain line at the end of Ch 07.
4. **Unmistakable HEA.** "I love you" and Kiss 3 in Ch 10. April coda shows them as a couple (Ray fixes the K; she lets him). Denise refuses to sell Ellen the "wedding date" square. Four kisses at most.
5. **Conditional promise.** Ch 03: "unless the numbers say otherwise," which Ray doesn't hear. Ch 06 argument is over what she actually promised.
6. **Comedy varied.** Pilot-dad bit cut from Ch 05. Ch 06 set piece belongs to Hollis. Ray's comic engines in Ch 02 (diagnosis by sound, the Bench), Ch 04 ("Fella I knew…"), Ch 08 (the Bench). Verna carries Ch 07. Ellen's ATC set pieces limited to Ch 01, 05, 09.
7. **One fewer weather crisis.** The Ch 06 boiler fails from age on an ordinary January night. Ch 04 nor'easter and Ch 09 storm kept.
8. **Ten chapters.** Ch 09 is storm/championship day and ends on the key. Ch 10 (~2,000) covers March 1 and the coda. Targets rebalanced to 32,000; overview, act breaks, POV plan, deadline table, romance beats, and threads updated.
9. **Cleanups.** Defecting teams return grumbling at $12.50, one sour line in Ch 09. Hollis–Judy seed at the lane 10 weigh-in. Gil's one line at the Open. Locker 14 resolved quietly in Ch 08. Denise's knowledge of the 2004 freeze dropped. Walk-ons unnamed. Ch 07 puts the 2 a.m. memory before the podium. Ray's $55,000 offer covers both the income and the cash gap.
